title: The man inside 'algorithm'
hook: Algorithm is a person's name, bent out of shape by medieval Latin.
peek: The word algorithm hides a 9th-century scholar from Baghdad, al-Khwarizmi. Latin translators turned his name into 'Algoritmi', and the same man's book on equations gave English the word algebra.
lede: Around the year 820, a scholar called Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi worked at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad. His surname means 'the one from Khwarazm', a region of Central Asia. He wrote a book explaining the Hindu-Arabic numerals and how to calculate with them. When Europeans translated it into Latin, his name came along, and slowly became a word for any step-by-step method.

bullets.text: A 12th-century Latin translation of his arithmetic book opens with 'Dixit Algoritmi', meaning 'Algoritmi says'. Its title is usually given as Algoritmi de numero Indorum, al-Khwarizmi on the numbers of the Indians.
In medieval Europe, 'algorism' meant reckoning with the new numerals instead of Roman numbers or a counting board. The th crept in later, probably by confusion with the Greek arithmos, number.

Al-Khwarizmi also wrote a book on solving equations with al-jabr in its title, meaning restoring or reuniting broken parts. That word became algebra, so one man gave English two of its central maths words.
For centuries algorithm simply meant a method of calculation. Only in the 20th century, with computing, did it come to mean the precise recipe of steps a machine follows.
